name: Asa
title: Reform King of Judah
summary: Asa ruled the kingdom of Judah for 41 years as the third king after the division of Israel. His reign was marked by profound religious reforms: he removed idols and cultic prostitution, deposed his grandmother Maaka as queen mother because she had made an Asherah image, and gathered the people for a solemn renewal of their covenant with the Lord. When an overwhelming Cushite army under Zerah threatened Judah, Asa placed his trust in God and won a decisive victory at Mareshah. His final years of rule were however overshadowed by failing faith. Faced with the threat from Israel's king Baasha, he chose to ally himself with Ben-Hadad of Aram-Damascus instead of seeking the Lord's help – and when the prophet Hanani rebuked him for this, Asa imprisoned the prophet in anger. Finally, he was struck by a serious foot disease, but even in this distress he turned to physicians rather than to God. Asa's story illustrates how faithful obedience early in life does not automatically guarantee faithfulness throughout one's entire life.

keyEvents.title: Asa Becomes King over Judah
keyEvents.description: Asa succeeded his father Abijam as king over Judah and reigned for 41 years in Jerusalem.

keyEvents.title: Victory over the Cushite army of Zerah
keyEvents.description: When a vast Cushite army under Zerah attacked Judah, Asa cried out to the Lord for help, and God gave him a mighty victory at Mareshah in the lowlands of Judah.

keyEvents.title: The Prophet Azariah's Encouragement
keyEvents.description: After the victory over the Cushites, the prophet Azariah son of Oded met with Asa and encouraged him to continue his reforms and remain faithful to the Lord. The prophet reminded him that the Lord would be with them as long as they were with Him.

keyEvents.title: Religious Reforms and Covenant Renewal
keyEvents.description: Asa carried out extensive religious reforms. He removed idols from the land, deposed Queen Mother Maacah because she had made an abhorrent Asherah image, and led the people in a solemn renewal of the covenant, where they swore to seek the Lord with all their heart and soul.

keyEvents.title: The Alliance with Aram against Israel
keyEvents.description: When Baasha, king of Israel, threatened Judah by fortifying Ramah, Asa sought help from Ben-Hadad of Aram instead of trusting in God. He took treasures from the temple and the royal palace to pay for the alliance.

keyEvents.title: The Prophet Hanani's Rebuke and Asa's Reaction
keyEvents.description: The seer Hanani rebuked Asa for relying on the king of Aram rather than on the Lord. Asa became furious, imprisoned Hanani, and at that time also oppressed some of the people.

keyEvents.title: Asa's Illness and Death
keyEvents.description: In his 39th year as king, Asa was afflicted with a serious foot disease, but even then he did not seek the Lord, only physicians. He died in his 41st year as king and was buried with great honor in the City of David.

versions.summary: Asa was the third king of Judah after the kingdom split. He is known for his religious reforms, during which he removed idolatry and renewed the covenant with God. Despite a good start, toward the end of his reign he showed a lack of trust in God by seeking help from Aram instead of the Lord.
versions.title: Judah's Reforming King
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Judas Reform King' is good and descriptive, but could optionally be clarified to include that he was the third king after the division. Nevertheless, the current title is concise and comprehensive.; [minor] Asa was also a religious reformer. The role 'reformer' could be added to reflect his central contribution to purifying worship in Judah.; [major] According to 1 Kings 15:10, Asa's mother (or grandmother) was Maacah, daughter of Absalom. Although the relationship is debated (some argue that 'mother' here means grandmother or queen mother), the Bible mentions her explicitly. The field should be filled with an appropriate reference.; [minor] The description notes that Asa removed his 'grandmother Maacah'. 1 Kings 15:13 uses the word 'mother' (Hebrew 'em'), but many scholars interpret this as grandmother or queen mother. The current wording is acceptable, but could clarify that the Hebrew term can mean both.; [minor] 1 Kings 15:9-10 is a correct reference for Asa's accession. Verse 15:8 could also be included to provide context for the transition from Abijam to Asa.; [major] Footnotes are missing. The profile would benefit from historical, archaeological, and theological notes on, for example, Asa's reforms, the Ethiopian invasion, the alliance with Aram, and the archaeological evidence for this period.

versions.summary: Asa was the third king of Judah after the kingdom split and reigned for 41 years. He is known for his extensive religious reforms, during which he removed idolatry, deposed Queen Mother Maacah, and renewed the covenant with God. The Lord gave him a mighty victory over a vast Cushite army. Despite a faithful beginning, toward the end of his reign he showed a lack of trust in God by seeking help from Aram instead of the Lord, and when he was struck by serious illness, he did not seek God's help either.
versions.title: Judah's Reforming King
versions.reason: [major] The reference 1 Kings 15:8-10 concerns Asa's accession, but the correct description of his accession is found in 1 Kings 15:9-10. Verse 8 deals primarily with Abijam's death. More importantly, 2 Chronicles 14:1-2 (bookId 14) also covers Asa's accession and should be included as a parallel reference.; [major] The reference 1 Kings 15:11-14 (bookId 11) is correct for the general reforms, but the renewal of the covenant and the removal of Maacah as queen mother are specifically mentioned in 1 Kings 15:13. Verses 11-14 are acceptable, but it could have been more precise to include verse 15, which mentions the dedication of gifts to the temple.; [minor] Maacah is referred to as Asa's 'mother' in 1 Kings 15:10, but as the linguistic footnote correctly points out, she was likely his grandmother (Abijam's mother). The value is acceptable since the Bible itself uses this designation, but it could have been helpful to note this in the profile.; [minor] Asa's wife is not named in the profile (spouse: null). According to 2 Chronicles 20:31, Jehoshaphat's mother was Azubah, daughter of Shilhi. She was thus Asa's wife and could have been included.; [minor] The title 'Reform King of Judah' is good and descriptive, but could have been somewhat more nuanced to capture both his reform work and his later weakening in faith. For example, 'Reformer King in Judah' is an alternative, but the current title works.; [minor] The summary is well formulated and covers the main points. It could have usefully mentioned that Asa imprisoned the prophet Hanani, which shows the seriousness of his late apostasy. Otherwise, it is a good and balanced presentation.; [minor] The role 'leader' is somewhat generic and overlaps with 'king'. Consider replacing it with 'commander' or 'military leader' given his role in the war against the Cushites.

versions.summary: Asa reigned as the third king of Judah after the kingdom was divided, for a total of 41 years. He carried out deep religious reforms by removing idolatry from the land, deposed his grandmother Maaka from her position as queen mother because of her idol worship, and led the people in a solemn renewal of the covenant with God. When an overwhelming Cushite army attacked, Asa cried out to the Lord and was granted a great victory at Mareshah. In his later years, however, his trust in God failed: he made an alliance with Aram-Damascus instead of seeking the Lord's help against Baesa king of Israel, and when the prophet Hanani confronted him about this, Asa reacted with anger and threw the prophet into prison. Stricken by a serious foot disease in his final years, he did not seek God's help then either, but only that of physicians.
versions.title: Reform King of Judah
versions.reason: [major] Maakah was actually Asa's grandmother (Abijam's mother), not his biological mother. Although the Hebrew 'em' can refer to both, the profile should ideally reflect this more clearly. Many scholars believe that Asa's actual mother is unknown from the text. At minimum, it should be noted that this refers to Maakah as queen mother/grandmother, not biological mother. A possible solution is to set mother to null and let the relationship with Maakah appear in keyEvents and footnotes.; [minor] Azubah (Azubah bat Shilhi) is mentioned as Jehoshaphat's mother in 1 Kings 22:42 and 2 Chronicles 20:31, and she is traditionally identified as Asa's wife. This is correct, but it may be worth noting that she is not directly named as Asa's wife in the text, only as Jehoshaphat's mother.; [minor] The footnote about the Ben-Hadad stele and the Tel Dan stele is somewhat imprecise. The Tel Dan stele likely mentions an Aramean king (possibly Hazael), but it dates from a slightly later period. The wording should be more cautious regarding the direct connection to Ben-Hadad I.; [major] The reference 1 Kings 15:8-10 (bookId 11, chapter 15, verses 8-10) is correct for Asa's accession. However, verse 8 concerns Abijam's death. It is more precise to start from verses 9-10 for the actual accession. In 2 Chronicles 14:1-2 (bookId 14, chapter 14, verses 1-2): verse 1 deals with Abijam's death and Asa's succession, while verse 2 states that Asa did what was right. The numbering in 2 Chronicles 14 varies between the Hebrew text and translations—in some counts, the chapter begins with what others consider 13:23. This should be verified.; [minor] The summary is good and theologically balanced. It covers both Asa's reforms, victory, weakening of trust, and illness. It is informative and well-phrased. A small adjustment is suggested for even better flow and to avoid similarity with earlier versions.; [minor] The lifespan 'c. 913–873 BC' refers to the reign period, not his entire life. It should be clarified that this is the reign period, e.g., 'reigned c. 913–873 BC', or that his birth year is unknown.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew word 'em' (אֵם) in 1 Kings 15:10 can mean both 'mother' and 'grandmother'. Many scholars believe that Maacah, referred to as Asa's mother, was actually his grandmother – that is, Abijam's mother – who continued to serve as queen mother (gebira) during Asa's reign until he deposed her.

Zerah (Hebrew: Zerah), who led the great army against Judah, is identified by some scholars with the Egyptian pharaoh Osorkon I or a Kushite military commander. The Kushite army of one million men (2 Chronicles 14:9) may reflect a major military expedition from Egypt's 22nd Dynasty, which had Libyan-Kushite origins.

Asa's religious reforms included the removal of cultic prostitution (Hebrew: qedeshim) and idols. This represented a return to pure Yahweh worship and was one of the most comprehensive religious purges in Judah's early history.

Aramaic inscriptions from the region, including the Tel Dan Stele, testify to the complex diplomatic network among the small states of the Levant during this period. Although the Tel Dan Stele likely dates from a somewhat later time and is associated with Hazael of Aram, it confirms Aramean political power and involvement in conflicts with Israel and Judah.

Asa's foot disease (2 Chronicles 16:12) has been discussed by biblical scholars and medical historians. Some suggest it may have been gout, diabetes-related gangrene, or peripheral vascular disease. The text emphasizes the theological point that he sought physicians rather than the Lord.

The covenant renewal under Asa (2 Chronicles 15:12–15) likely took place in the third month, possibly in connection with the Feast of Weeks (Shavuot). The renewal included an oath to seek the Lord with all one's heart, and the death penalty for anyone who did not seek the God of Israel – a pattern rooted in Deuteronomic covenant theology.

The gebira role (queen mother) was a formal institution in the kingdom of Judah with significant political and religious influence. The fact that Asa deposed Maacah from this position (1 Kings 15:13; 2 Chronicles 15:16) underscores the radical nature of his reform program, as it involved breaking with powerful dynastic structures.

Mareshah (Tell Sandahanna), where Asa defeated the Kushite army, was an important fortified city in the Judean lowlands (Shephelah). Archaeological excavations have uncovered significant fortification structures from the Iron Age at the site, confirming the city's strategic importance.
